prompt.context: It is 2005 and your client is a Private Equity firm looking to purchase an HDTV Remote Control manufacturing company. The firm would like to sell the company after 3 years.
prompt.question: Should they go forward with the acquisition?

clarifying_info.a: There are 2 main players but otherwise fragmented.

clarifying_info.q: What are the target company's revenues?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues for the last 3 years have been $25M, $50M, and $100M.

clarifying_info.q: What is the target's market share?
clarifying_info.a: They have maintained a 25% market share throughout.

clarifying_info.q: What is the selling price per unit?

clarifying_info.a: You can assume margins are attractive.

clarifying_info.q: How long will the transition from normal TVs to HDTVs take?
clarifying_info.a: The client expects that all normal TVs will be replaced by HDTVs and from start to finish this will take 9 years.

framework: Market attractiveness: size, growth rate, competitive landscape
Target company analysis: revenues, costs, market share, product, growth trajectory
PE firm perspective: acquisition strategy, synergies, ROI, exit multiples, risks
Market sizing: start with US households, derive total TVs, estimate HDTV adoption rate
Exit analysis: assess entry multiple vs. exit multiple given where the company sits in the growth cycle

questions.prompt: Size the US HDTV remote control market.
questions.guidance: Candidate should link TV remotes to TVs sold, not just TV stock. Key insight: HDTV adoption is driven by technology desire, not TV breakdowns, so the replacement cycle is faster than a normal 10-year TV life. Walk through: 300M people / 3 people per HH = 100M HH; 100M HH x 3 TVs = 300M TVs. From the revenue data provided (target has 25% share, remotes at $10 each): Year 1 revenue $25M implies 2.5M units sold by target, so total market = 10M units = $100M. Year 2 revenue $50M implies $200M market. Year 3 revenue $100M implies $400M market. Market growing 100% YoY.

math.setup: Target revenues: $25M, $50M, $100M at 25% market share, $10/remote. Derive total market revenues and unit volumes.
steps: Total TVs to be converted: 300M. Already converted (approx): 10M + 20M + 40M = 70M in first 3 years. Remaining: ~230M TVs over 6 remaining years, average ~38M/year but front-loaded.
math.answer: Market has grown 100% YoY; $100M -> $200M -> $400M. Total US TV stock is 300M; HDTV conversion expected over 9 years with front-loaded adoption.

questions.prompt: How would you expect the HDTV remote control market to behave over the next 6 years (years 4-9 of the adoption cycle)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should describe an S-curve or bell-curve adoption pattern: slow start (already seen in years 1-3), rapid acceleration as momentum builds (peak in years 4-6), then tapering off as the remaining population adopts and the stock of normal TVs is exhausted. Candidate should draw this as a curve that peaks and then declines toward zero as adoption completes. Key: volumes will still be high in years 1-3 post-acquisition (2005-2008) but will start declining thereafter.

math.setup: 300M total TVs; ~70M converted in years 1-3; ~230M remaining over years 4-9; average ~38M/year but front-loaded.
steps: But adoption is front-loaded: peak likely years 4-5, then declining
By sell date (2008 = year 6 of adoption), market will be near or past peak
math.answer: Market likely peaks around 2006-2007, then declines. At 2008 sell date, the company will be entering or already in a declining phase.

questions.prompt: Given the timing of acquisition (2005) and planned exit (2008), assess whether the PE firm should acquire the company.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will identify the valuation timing problem: In 2005 the company is in a high-growth phase, commanding high revenue multiples. By 2008, the HDTV transition will be largely complete and growth will be slowing or negative, so the company will command low multiples at exit. Even if the company is profitable, the PE firm buys at peak multiples and sells at trough multiples - destroying value. This is the core insight.

math.setup: Qualitative multiple compression analysis: buy at high multiple (growth phase), sell at low multiple (declining phase).
steps: 2002-2004: High growth phase = high revenue/EBITDA multiples
2005 (acquisition date): Company still in high-growth phase; seller will demand high multiple
2005-2007: Sustained growth continues; company performs well
2008 (sell date): HDTV transition ~75%+ complete; growth slowing; multiples compress
math.answer: The PE firm would buy at high multiples (growth stage) and sell at low multiples (maturity/decline stage). This multiple compression makes the deal unattractive despite the company's profitability.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should the PE firm consider when evaluating this acquisition?

categories.name: Market risks
ideas: HDTV adoption rate slower than expected, extending the growth phase
Competition from TV manufacturers bundling remotes, reducing aftermarket demand
Commoditization risk and price pressure as market matures
New technology (e.g., universal remotes, smartphone-based control) disrupting standalone remotes

categories.name: Target company risks
ideas: Customer concentration if dependent on few TV makers or retailers
Manufacturing cost structure and ability to scale
Intellectual property or proprietary technology advantage
Quality and reliability of revenue figures

categories.name: PE / deal structure risks
ideas: Purchase price multiple paid relative to growth outlook
Ability to find a buyer in 2008 at acceptable exit multiple
Operational improvements possible within 3-year hold period
Leverage / debt service constraints on operations

recommendation: Do NOT proceed with the acquisition

Despite the target's strong revenue growth (100% YoY) and attractive margins, the PE firm would be acquiring at peak valuation multiples in 2005 and forced to exit in 2008 as the HDTV market approaches saturation and growth decelerates
Multiple compression between buy (high-growth premium) and sell (low-growth/decline discount) will destroy value even if the underlying business performs well
risks: If HDTV adoption takes longer than 9 years, the exit in 2008 could still be at a high-growth multiple — but this is uncertain
If a strategic buyer (e.g., TV manufacturer) values synergies, exit multiple may be partially protected
next_steps: If the firm still wants to pursue, negotiate a significantly lower entry multiple to offset multiple compression at exit
Model out scenario analysis on adoption curve timing
Explore whether operational improvements or market share gains could offset multiple compression
